Create a cinematic steampunk movie title reading HALVER, with THE WINDOW MAKER in small, simple serif typography underneath.
The silhouette of HALVER is the priority.
Shape the six separate letters into a strong hourglass / bow-tie silhouette using the letters themselves:
H and R are the tallest
A and E are slightly shorter
L and V are the shortest at the center
the upper edges gradually dip toward the middle
the lower edges rise toward the middle
This creates two opposite arcs pinching toward the center.
Do not add any continuous line, rail, border, frame, arch or base connecting the letters. The curved silhouette must come entirely from the individual letter shapes.
Each letter is an independent, deep 3D construction made from different antique windows — brass, iron, aged wood, arched windows, circular windows and rectangular windows.
Connect the separate letters only with individual exposed steampunk pipes, elbows, valves and fittings. Add layered gears, cogs, machinery, vents and escaping steam behind and between the letters. Give the entire title strong physical depth, foreground/background layering and cinematic shadows.
Inside the windows show different miniature worlds and moments, including:
laundry room with a woman folding clothes
two people sitting on a porch at sunset
colorful candy shop
simple interior floor
open sea
Tuscany villa
bright green field
mountains and nature
city streets
warm interiors
Every window should feel like a different memory, place or moment, rather than repeating the same landscape.
Dark atmospheric background, warm window light, realistic brass and wood materials, drifting steam, deep shadows, cinematic steampunk fantasy, intricate but elegant.
THE WINDOW MAKER centered beneath HALVER, clean and understated.
No ornament, flourish, decorative line or emblem beneath the subtitle.
Create a sunset version of this change the shadow direction

Create a professional cinematic prop-design sheet for a fictional late-Victorian currency system.
Show exactly THREE different coins:
1 coin
5 coin
10 coin
Each denomination must appear in THREE views:
FRONT FACE
REVERSE FACE
SIDE / EDGE PROFILE
Arrange the sheet in three clean horizontal rows:
ROW 1 — 1 coin
front face → reverse face → side profile
ROW 2 — 5 coin
front face → reverse face → side profile
ROW 3 — 10 coin
front face → reverse face → side profile
NO written labels, titles, captions, material names, measurements, or explanatory text anywhere on the sheet.
The only typography allowed is the denomination numeral physically engraved into the FRONT face of the coin:
1
5
10
The reverse faces contain NO denomination numbers.
All three coins belong to the same fictional Victorian-era currency system, but every denomination has its own distinct design, material, thickness, edge treatment, and level of ornamentation.
1 COIN
Smallest and simplest denomination.
Material:
aged inexpensive copper / bronze.
FRONT:
large engraved numeral “1” centered on the coin.
Victorian botanical wreath surrounding the denomination.
Fine beaded outer rim.
Restrained decorative flourishes.
Simple working-class everyday currency design.
REVERSE:
a different composition from the front.
Elegant Victorian monogram or simple civic emblem.
Botanical wreath or restrained floral engraving.
No numeral.
EDGE:
thin coin.
Distinct repeating diamond or geometric stamped pattern around the entire edge.
Copper coloration must match across front, reverse, and edge views.
5 COIN
Medium denomination.
Material:
aged brass.
Slightly larger and thicker than the 1 coin.
FRONT:
large engraved numeral “5”.
Ornate circular Victorian frame.
Small crown above the denomination.
Industrial imagery subtly integrated into the design:
factory architecture,
chimneys,
steam machinery,
small locomotive elements.
Decorative scrollwork fills the lower and outer areas.
REVERSE:
completely different design while remaining part of the same currency family.
Victorian civic / industrial emblem.
Mechanical wheel, architectural structure, workshop or industrial symbol.
Laurel branches and ornamental scrollwork.
No numeral.
EDGE:
medium thickness.
Fine vertical reeded edge running continuously around the circumference.
Brass coloration must remain identical between front, reverse, and edge views.
10 COIN
Largest and most prestigious denomination.
Material:
inexpensive silvery nickel alloy / nickel silver / pewter-like metal.
Largest diameter and slightly thicker than the 5 coin.
FRONT:
large engraved numeral “10” inside an ornate heraldic cartouche.
Two classical Victorian allegorical figures flank the denomination.
Small crown above.
Detailed late-19th-century city and industrial architecture beneath.
Highly refined engraved ornamentation.
Formal but still believable as circulating everyday currency.
REVERSE:
a detailed Victorian heraldic coat of arms.
Central shield.
Two heraldic animals supporting the shield.
Crown above.
Decorative floral scrollwork and small mechanical or civic emblem beneath.
No numeral.
EDGE:
thicker decorative edge.
Continuous engraved Victorian floral-scroll pattern around the circumference.
The edge design must clearly correspond to the same physical 10 coin.
DESIGN CONSISTENCY
The FRONT, REVERSE, and SIDE view of each denomination must represent the exact same physical coin.
Do not redesign the coin between views.
Maintain identical:
diameter,
thickness,
metal color,
rim shape,
wear level,
engraving depth,
and manufacturing style.
The side profile must clearly show the actual edge pattern described for that denomination.
The three denominations should increase logically in visual importance:
1 = simple
5 = more decorative
10 = most elaborate
However, they must still feel like one coherent national currency produced during the same historical period.
HISTORICAL STYLE
Believable late-19th-century Victorian minting.
Fine mechanical engraving.
Stamped relief.
Raised rims.
Period-appropriate ornamental language.
Subtle heraldic influence.
Botanical decoration.
Industrial symbolism.
The designs may have a restrained industrial-fantasy character, but they must remain historically plausible.
Do not make them look like fantasy medallions, commemorative tokens, casino chips, or modern collectible coins.
MATERIAL CONDITION
The coins should look clean and production-ready for a film prop department.
Light natural patina only.
Fine realistic metal variation.
No heavy scratches.
No corrosion.
No rust.
No damaged rims.
No extreme tarnish.
No dirt.
No ancient archaeological appearance.
They should look circulated but well maintained.
PROP SHEET PRESENTATION
Straight-on orthographic presentation for front and reverse faces.
Side views photographed almost perfectly level with the edge.
Neutral warm off-white studio background.
Soft professional product-photography lighting.
Very subtle contact shadows.
No dramatic environment.
No hands.
No coin stacks.
No boxes.
No additional props.
Precise spacing.
Each row clearly separated through composition only.
Consistent camera angle and scale.
High-resolution realistic metal detail.
Film-production concept art / prop department reference photography.
16:9 horizontal composition.
ABSOLUTELY NO TEXT ON THE PROP SHEET.
Only the engraved denomination numerals 1, 5, and 10 may appear, and only on the corresponding FRONT faces of the coins.
